findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Base stale classification on an actual last-convergence time (e.g. the commit/committer time of the old remote-tracking tip or merge-base, or a recorded last-fetch stamp), not only the oldest unpushed event ts, or explicitly document why the proxy is an accepted deviation from ADR §5; add a fixture for an old convergence with a recent unpushed write.
evidence: Context: 'a clone whose last convergence predates the N-day reclaim horizon OVERRIDE its local tickets'
Approach 2: 'Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.'
Testing covers only 'only unpushed event is older than the horizon' and 'unpushed event inside the horizon'. It has no case of an old last convergence with a recent write.
findings.finding: The stale classification proxy (oldest unpushed event ts < now − horizon) does not implement the ADR §5 condition it cites ('last convergence predates the N-day horizon'). The I5 argument runs the wrong way. Oldest-unpushed-ts being old implies stale, but a clone that last converged 60 days ago and wrote yesterday (push failed offline or against the rewritten remote) has a recent oldest unpushed event. It is classified fresh and its events are replayed, although ADR §5 says such a clone must be overridden.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh' vs Context/Problem (ADR 0106 §5)
scenarios: A laptop is offline for 60 days, the user makes an edit yesterday, then reconnects after a reclaim. The edit is classified fresh and replayed onto the reclaimed baseline, based on a 60-day-stale view.
findings.suggested_fix: Define last convergence as the committer timestamp of the local remote-tracking ref's tip before fetch (the last remote state this clone merged). Classify stale iff min(that time, oldest unpushed ts) < now − horizon_days.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either base staleness on a true last-convergence signal (e.g. the committer time of the last commit shared with the pre-swap remote, or a recorded last-successful-sync stamp), or state explicitly that the plan narrows ADR 0106 §5 and why replaying recent-but-long-offline writes is safe. Add a test for the 'long offline, recent write' case.
evidence: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days`"
"Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
ADR 0106 §5 is cited as requiring override when 'last convergence predates the N-day reclaim horizon'.
findings.finding: The stale classification is a one-sided bound and diverges from ADR 0106 §5's criterion ('last convergence predates the N-day horizon'). The oldest unpushed event's ts is an UPPER bound on last convergence. So 'oldest unpushed < now−horizon' does imply stale, but 'oldest unpushed ≥ now−horizon' does not imply fresh. A clone offline for 60 days whose only writes happened yesterday is classified fresh and replays, although the ADR says it should be overridden.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh'
scenarios: A laptop is offline for two months with no tickets edits, then makes one edit the day before reconnecting. It is classified fresh and its event is replayed onto the reclaimed baseline, contrary to the ADR's override rule.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Align the stale/fresh rule with parent 536b's C3 ('last remote convergence older than N days'), either by measuring convergence directly (e.g. the last fetched remote tip's commit time) or by updating the parent to adopt the oldest-unpushed-event proxy, and make sure in-horizon unpushed events of a recently converged clone are never discarded.
evidence: Leaf: 'The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days` … Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.'
Leaf: 'A stale clone replays nothing and logs a WARNING naming the backup ref and the discarded event count'
Parent C3: 'any clone whose last remote convergence is older than N days is forced to reset local `tickets` to remote on reconnect and may NOT reintroduce E by merge/rebase.'
Parent mechanism: 'live clones (< N days) merge normally at swap; staler clones are refused a reintroducing merge and reset to remote (accepted loss).'
Parent AC: 'C1–C5 proven to prevent resurrection across all clone states, incl. a <N-day clone with unpushed writes.'

Unpushed-event ts is at best a one-sided bound on convergence time (an unpushed event is always newer than the last convergence). It does not tell you when the clone last fetched, and nothing in the leaf records a convergence watermark.
findings.finding: The leaf changes how the parent decides whether a clone is stale. The parent says a clone is stale when its LAST REMOTE CONVERGENCE is older than N days. The leaf uses a different test: the clone is stale when its OLDEST UNPUSHED EVENT's ts is older than the horizon, and then it decides once for the whole clone (replay everything or discard everything). This disagrees with the parent's guarantee for live clones. A clone that converged recently but still holds one old unpushed event (for example, a push that kept failing) is called stale and loses ALL of its unpushed work, including events written inside the horizon. A clone whose last convergence is older than N days but whose only unpushed writes are recent is called fresh and keeps its work. Divergence kind: redefines a parent deliverable (contradicts_reality candidate), unless the parent is updated to adopt the proxy.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh' and step 4 'Fresh clones replay; stale clones do not'; parent epic 536b C3 clause
scenarios: A clone fetches daily but one event's push was rejected 35 days ago. At reconnect after the swap it is classified stale, and its yesterday's events are discarded even though it converged yesterday.

A clone was offline for 40 days and wrote one event this morning. It is classified fresh and replays, which the parent's '>N-day offline clones lose divergent work' rule would forbid (harmless for resurrection, but it is not the parent's contract).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' stating, per override step (backup ref, reset, replay commit, push), whether failure is retryable (left for the next sync tick) or fatal. State that a failure before the HEAD move leaves HEAD untouched and reports DIVERGED.
evidence: "in `_do_reconverge`'s unrelated-history branch, call the override when the remote supersedes; otherwise keep the existing refusal unchanged."
A disposition is stated only for malformed lineage ('fails closed like a malformed `epoch`') and for stale discard ('logs a WARNING'); no step-failure disposition is stated for the override itself.
findings.finding: The plan replaces the DIVERGED refusal with a new multi-step override arm but never states the disposition when a step of that arm fails. Unstated cases include failure to create the backup ref, `reset --hard` failure, replay-commit failure, and a push failure of the replayed commit. The plan does not say whether each is retryable on the next sync tick or fatal, nor whether the caller falls back to DIVERGED with HEAD untouched.
findings.location: Approach (override steps 1-4); Scope `src/rebar/_store/sync.py` unrelated-history branch
scenarios: `update-ref` for the backup fails: it is unstated whether the reset still proceeds, which would make the loss unrecoverable, or whether the run aborts and reports DIVERGED.
The replayed commit's push is rejected: it is unstated whether this is retryable by the normal push path or surfaced as a blocking divergence via freshness.write_blocking_divergence.
findings.suggested_fix: State: any failure before the HEAD move aborts with HEAD untouched and keeps today's DIVERGED disposition, which is retried on the next sync. The reset is never attempted unless the backup ref was written. A push failure of the replay commit stays retryable through the existing push path, as for any unpushed local write.

evidence: 2 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.finding: Acceptance-criteria / definition-of-done quality issues.
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build stale_override's event parsing on the shared filename helpers (`reducer._sort.prefix_ts`, `reducer._cache.RETIRED_SUFFIX`/`is_active_event`) instead of a private regex. Treat every non-dot file under a ticket dir as an event candidate (including `-PRECONDITIONS-SNAPSHOT.json`), and add a test with a hyphenated-type event.
evidence: Plan: "Parse event filenames per the I2 contract (`{ts}-{uuid}-{TYPE}.json`, optional `.retired`; `docs/event-schema.md:14-29`)."
src/rebar/reducer/_sort.py:7-8: "``prefix_ts`` is the single shared comparator the other filename-order sites ... import."
src/rebar/reducer/_cache.py:14-17: `RETIRED_SUFFIX = ".retired"` described as the "shared suffix [that] keeps compaction and reducer scans aligned", plus `is_active_event()` at :20.
src/rebar/reducer/_version.py:94 `KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` is the single source of event-type names.
PRECONDITIONS-SNAPSHOT event names exist: src/rebar/reducer/_api.py:73,97; reducer/_inbound.py:53; _ids.py:219; _snapshot/ticket_objects.py:195.
stale_override.py:48 `-(?P<type>[A-Z_]+)\.json(?P<retired>\.retired)?$`: a hyphenated type does not match, and `_events()` skips non-matching names at :161-163.
findings.finding: The plan's step 1 ('Parse event filenames per the I2 contract') is done with a new module-private regex (`_EVENT_RE` in stale_override.py) instead of the filename helpers the codebase already shares for this purpose. The copy has already drifted: `(?P<type>[A-Z_]+)\.json` cannot match the existing `{ts}-{uuid}-PRECONDITIONS-SNAPSHOT.json` event names, so `_events()` skips them silently. A fresh clone's unpushed PRECONDITIONS-SNAPSHOT event would never be counted or replayed, and it would be lost after `reset --hard` without appearing in the discarded count.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (Local-only events) / src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:45-49
scenarios: A fresh clone with an unpushed `...-PRECONDITIONS-SNAPSHOT.json` reconnects after a publish-swap. The file is not in `unpushed`, so it is not replayed. `reset --hard` deletes it from the working tree and the WARNING reports zero discarded events.
A future event type, or a change to the I2 contract, is updated in reducer/_sort.py and _cache.py but not in stale_override's private regex, and the override starts skipping those files silently.
findings.suggested_fix: Get ts from `reducer._sort.prefix_ts(name)` and the retired flag from `name.endswith(RETIRED_SUFFIX)`. Get the uuid as the fixed-width 36-character UUID that follows the first '-', and the type as the remainder up to '.json', so hyphenated types are kept. Or factor one shared `parse_event_name()` into the reducer helpers and import it here and in fsck_repair.py:171-177, which also splits names by hand.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add fsck_tracker_health._classify_sync to Scope: classify a superseding-epoch unrelated remote separately from DIVERGED (e.g. 'reclaimed baseline pending; next sync overrides'), or explicitly state in the plan that it stays DIVERGED and why.
evidence: fsck_tracker_health.py:153: 'Mirrors the divergence taxonomy in ``_store/sync.py``'
fsck_tracker_health.py:214-221: an unrelated history always returns a DIVERGED issue telling the user to run fsck-recover or re-clone and re-init.
Plan Approach: unrelated histories whose remote epoch supersedes the local one are now overridden, not refused, so sync's taxonomy has a new branch that fsck does not mirror.
findings.finding: fsck still reports a superseding-epoch rewrite as 'DIVERGED ... built independently ... Recover: run `rebar store fsck-recover`, or re-clone and re-init'. Its docstring says it mirrors the divergence taxonomy in _store/sync.py, and this plan changes that taxonomy. The plan does not list it as a consumer to update.
findings.location: src/rebar/_commands/fsck_tracker_health.py:_tracker_sync_status/_classify_sync (not in Scope)
scenarios: An operator runs `rebar store fsck` on a clone that has not yet reconverged after a reclaim swap. fsck reports a DIVERGED issue and recommends fsck-recover or re-init, which contradicts the new protocol in docs/concurrency.md.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add freshness.write_blocking_divergence / _seam._refuse_unpublishable_store to Scope. Either have them recognise a superseding-epoch remote (point to sync or reconverge, not fsck-recover/maintenance), or record in the plan why leaving them unchanged is safe.
evidence: Plan Context: 'Such a clone stays wedged forever, its writes are refused by `freshness.write_blocking_divergence`, and a manual repair risks the resurrection ... that the horizon exists to prevent.'
freshness.py:235-253: write_blocking_divergence returns verdict 'diverged' whenever `merge-base HEAD remote_ref` fails, with no check of compat.remote_epoch_supersedes_local.
_seam.py:400-407: refusal text 'Run `rebar store fsck` to confirm DIVERGED ...; recover with `rebar store fsck-recover` ... or use `rebar store maintenance`'.
Scope lists only stale_override.py, compat.py, sync.py, the test file and docs/concurrency.md.
findings.finding: After a publish-swap, the write path still treats a clone whose remote provably supersedes it as an unrecoverable split and points the user to manual repair. The plan names this as part of the problem but leaves it out of Scope. freshness.write_blocking_divergence refuses on any missing merge-base, and _seam._refuse_unpublishable_store tells the user to run `rebar store fsck-recover` or `rebar store maintenance`. It does not say that the next sync will apply the reclaimed-baseline override.
findings.location: Scope (missing src/rebar/_store/freshness.py and src/rebar/_commands/_seam.py); Context: 'its writes are refused by freshness.write_blocking_divergence'
scenarios: A user writes to a ticket on a clone right after the swap and before any read has triggered reconverge. The write is refused and the message points to fsck-recover/maintenance, which is the manual repair that can resurrect reclaimed events, instead of saying a sync will move the clone onto the reclaimed baseline.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in Approach step 2 that the filename `ts` is an HLC prefix (event-schema.md:20-24) and not pure wall time. Then either justify comparing it to `now − horizon` (HLC only errs toward 'fresh', and replaying events the remote doesn't know about cannot resurrect anything) or classify by a wall-clock source instead.
evidence: Plan: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days`"

docs/event-schema.md:20-24 — '`${timestamp_ns}` — a single-integer Hybrid Logical Clock prefix ... `max(per-clone cache, the target ticket's witnessed max-prefix, time_ns()) + 1`. It tracks wall-clock ns but never ties or inverts'
stale_override.py:216-220 — cutoff computed from `datetime.now(UTC)` in ns, compared directly with the HLC prefix
findings.finding: Stale classification compares the event filename `ts` with `now − horizon` as if `ts` were wall-clock time. Under the I2 contract the plan cites, the prefix is a Hybrid Logical Clock: `max(per-clone cache, the target ticket's witnessed max-prefix, time_ns()) + 1`. It can run ahead of wall time once a clone has seen a future-skewed prefix. The plan never states that it assumes HLC ≈ wall-clock, and that it can only make a clone look fresher than it is, never staler.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh'; Approach step 1 cites docs/event-schema.md:14-29
scenarios: A ticket gets an event written by a clone whose clock runs fast. A stale clone that later wrote to that ticket carries an HLC prefix inflated past real time. Its old unpushed events count as inside the horizon, so it replays instead of being overridden as ADR 0106 §5 requires.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to step 2: "`ts` is the I2 HLC prefix; it never lags wall time, so skew can only classify a stale clone as fresh, which replays only uuids unknown to the remote and therefore cannot resurrect reclaimed events."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Strengthen the pre-epoch case of the lineage proof (e.g. require an additional identity check such as a ticket-id/uuid overlap or a store-id when the matched lineage entry is null) and add a fixture: pre-epoch local vs an unrelated remote whose lineage contains null → DIVERGED.
evidence: 'whose new epoch_lineage list names the local epoch (JSON null stands for the pre-epoch/absent record). That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store, so unrelated stores keep today's refusal.'
The Testing 'unrelated remote' case uses a 'different epoch' local, not a pre-epoch local against a null-lineage unrelated remote.
findings.finding: Using JSON null in epoch_lineage for pre-epoch stores weakens the 'proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store'. Every store that was pre-epoch before its first reclaim will carry null in its lineage. A pre-epoch clone pointed at any such reclaimed remote, even an unrelated store, will therefore pass `remote_epoch_supersedes_local` and be reset --hard. Today almost all stores are pre-epoch, so this is the common first-reclaim path rather than an edge.
findings.location: Approach para 1 (lineage proof) / compat.py remote_epoch_supersedes_local
scenarios: A pre-epoch clone has its remote URL repointed (by misconfiguration) at another project's reclaimed tickets branch. The local tickets are reset --hard to a foreign store instead of being refused as DIVERGED.
findings.suggested_fix: When the local epoch is null, additionally require that the remote tip shares at least one ticket directory (or event uuid / SNAPSHOT source_event_uuid) with local HEAD before treating the remote as superseding. Otherwise keep the DIVERGED refusal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the fresh-path override atomic or resumable: build the replay commit object on top of the pinned remote first (e.g. via a temporary index/commit-tree) and only then move HEAD in one ref update, or record an in-progress marker that the next reconverge resumes; add a fault-injection test between reset and replay.
evidence: 'Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD ... then reset --hard to the pinned remote commit.'
'A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote'
There is no step for resuming or detecting an interrupted override.
findings.finding: The override sequence (backup ref → reset --hard → replay commit) is not crash-safe or idempotent for fresh clones. If the process dies or the replay commit fails after the reset, HEAD equals the remote. The next reconverge then finds a merge-base and never re-enters the override path, so the unpushed events survive only in the backup ref and are silently not delivered.
findings.location: Approach steps 3-4 / stale_override.py
scenarios: SIGKILL, disk-full or a commit-hook failure between `reset --hard` and the replay commit loses a fresh clone's recent writes without any WARNING.
findings.suggested_fix: Construct the replay tree and commit (parent = pinned remote commit) with plumbing before touching HEAD. Then do a single `update-ref`/`reset --hard <replay-commit>`, so there is never an intermediate state where HEAD equals the remote without the replay.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State (and test) the invariant the reclaim must guarantee for unpushed detection — e.g. every removed uuid is transitively listed in a surviving SNAPSHOT's source_event_uuids — or restrict 'unpushed' to events not reachable from the local remote-tracking ref (git-based, not uuid-based); add fixtures for chained snapshots and a fully reclaimed ticket.
evidence: 'A local event is unpushed iff its uuid appears nowhere on the remote tip — not as a file under the ticket dir (any suffix), and not in any remote SNAPSHOT's data.source_event_uuids for that ticket'
The no-resurrection fixture covers only a single remote retire or a single SNAPSHOT fold, not chained snapshots or a dropped ticket.
findings.finding: Unpushed detection treats any local event uuid absent from the remote tip (as a file or in a SNAPSHOT's source_event_uuids) as unpushed. That is only true if the reclaim always records every removed uuid in a surviving SNAPSHOT's source_event_uuids for that ticket. Three cases may break this: chained snapshots that list only the delta since the previous snapshot, reclaimed or deleted whole tickets, and retired files dropped by the reclaim. In those cases already-pushed old events appear unpushed. They then (a) force a genuinely fresh clone into the stale branch, discarding its recent writes, or (b) get replayed and resurrect history.
findings.location: Approach step 1 'Local-only events' / Testing 'No resurrection'
scenarios: A fresh clone holds a pre-horizon event folded into an older SNAPSHOT that a newer SNAPSHOT superseded without re-listing. That event counts as 'unpushed' with an old ts, so the clone is classified stale and its yesterday's write is discarded.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute unpushed events as files added in commits reachable from local HEAD but not from the pre-fetch remote-tracking ref (`git log refs/remotes/<r>/tickets..HEAD --name-only`). Then use the remote-tip uuid/SNAPSHOT check only as a second no-resurrection filter.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document in docs/concurrency.md a safe restore procedure for `refs/rebar/stale-override/*` (e.g. cherry-pick specific event files, never merge), and specify stamp-collision handling (e.g. suffix with a uuid) and retention for these refs.
evidence: 'Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed)'
AC 4 lists docs content 'lineage proof, stale classification, backup ref, accepted loss' but no restore procedure.
findings.finding: Several back-out details for the destructive reset are unspecified. The backup ref is the only rollback path, but the plan gives no restore procedure (how an operator recovers discarded stale events from `refs/rebar/stale-override/*` without re-introducing reclaimed history). It also does not cover collision handling for two overrides in the same UTC second, or retention and cleanup of accumulating backup refs.
findings.location: Approach step 3 / docs/concurrency.md scope
scenarios: A user whose stale writes were discarded needs them back. Without a documented safe procedure, a naive merge of the backup ref resurrects reclaimed events.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the backup-ref stamp format (ref-name-safe, e.g. `%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ`, plus a uniqueness suffix) and a retirement path (prune after N days or a documented manual-removal command) in stale_override.py and docs/concurrency.md.
evidence: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed)"
The plan names no expiry, prune command, or gc policy for these refs.
findings.finding: The backup ref `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` is created on every override but has no RETIRE/cleanup path. The stamp format and uniqueness are also unspecified: an ISO-8601 stamp with ':' is an invalid git ref name, and two overrides in the same second would collide or overwrite.
findings.location: Approach step 3 'Backup, then override'
scenarios: A clone that reconnects after each of several reclaims accumulates backup refs indefinitely. Each one pins pre-collapse history locally and defeats local gc of the reclaimed objects.
A stamp rendered as `2025-01-01T00:00:00Z` fails `git update-ref` because ':' is forbidden in ref names, so the backup step errors before the reset.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a ref-safe stamp such as `20250101T000000Z-<short-old-head-sha>`. Document in docs/concurrency.md that these refs are local recovery artifacts, and either prune them once older than `[reclaim].horizon_days` during the next override, or name the `git update-ref -d` command for removing them.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make override+replay a single atomic HEAD move: build the replay commit (parent = pinned remote) before touching HEAD, then reset once to it. Add a test that interrupts between backup and HEAD move and asserts the next reconverge still replays.
evidence: "Point ... at the old local HEAD ..., then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit."
"A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files byte-identically ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
The override is triggered only 'when HEAD and the remote share no merge-base'; after the reset that condition is false.
findings.finding: The override is not atomic or idempotent across a crash between step 3 (`reset --hard` to the remote) and step 4 (the fresh replay commit). On the next reconverge HEAD equals the remote and a merge-base exists, so the override branch never runs again. The fresh clone's unpushed events then survive only in the backup ref, with no replay and no WARNING.
findings.location: Approach steps 3-4; Scope `src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py`
scenarios: The process is killed (OOM, SIGTERM, laptop sleep) after the reset but before the replay commit. A fresh clone's legitimate unpushed writes are silently dropped, which is exactly the loss the fresh path exists to prevent.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the replay commit off-HEAD first: build its tree with a temporary index or `git commit-tree`, using the pinned remote commit as parent. Then create the backup ref and perform a single `reset --hard` to the replay commit, or to the remote commit when there is nothing to replay. This leaves only one state transition, so no intermediate state loses events.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the 'every write auto-pushes (I5)' rationale in Approach step 2 with a premise the code actually backs. Either measure last convergence directly (e.g., a last-successful-reconverge/fetch marker or the newest remote-known event in HEAD), or document that best-effort, `off` and `async` push leave old unpushed events on clones that still converge, and accept that loss explicitly.
evidence: Plan: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
docs/concurrency.md:272 — '### I5 — Single locked write path' (about the write lock, not push)

docs/concurrency.md:576 — 'Push is best-effort by default. A failed push caused by network loss, unresolved non-fast-forward state, or a recovery state does not fail existing callers. It warns and preserves local commits.' / PUSH_PENDING backlog
docs/concurrency.md:750-755 — `sync.push` policies `async`/`off`; `rebar store import` uses `off` for its whole run
stale_override.py:98 — `stale = bool(unpushed) and min(event.ts for event in unpushed) < cutoff`
findings.finding: The stale/fresh rule rests on 'Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.' The code and docs don't support this. I5 in docs/concurrency.md is 'Single locked write path' (lock-guarded append/commit) and says nothing about pushing. The auto-push contract (concurrency.md:576) is best-effort: a failed push 'warns and preserves local commits', which fsck reports as PUSH_PENDING, and inbound sync keeps converging. `sync.push` also supports `off` and `async`, and `rebar store import` runs with `off` until it finishes. So an old unpushed event does not show that the clone's last convergence predates the horizon.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh' (and the matching sentence in docs/concurrency.md:810-812)
scenarios: A clone with push failing for weeks (permission denied, or the remote rejecting it) while fetch/reconverge still works: it converged recently but has unpushed events older than the horizon. After the swap it is classified stale and that work is silently dropped (kept only in the local backup ref).
A clone with `sync.push = off` (or an interrupted bulk import) that converges inbound regularly has its pending events treated as stale.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the whole-clone 'oldest unpushed event' stale test with a classification that does not throw away in-horizon work because of one old event (e.g. classify per ticket directory), and restate the rationale without the claim that the oldest unpushed write bounds last convergence.
evidence: Plan: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days`"
Plan: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
docs/concurrency.md I5 describes the locked write path; push is best-effort, and sync's fetch/merge (_do_reconverge) runs independently of push success.
src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:98 `stale = bool(unpushed) and min(event.ts for event in unpushed) < cutoff` discards every unpushed event when any single one is old.
ADR 0106 §5 defines stale by last convergence (merge-base vs checkpoint), not by the age of the oldest unpushed write.
findings.finding: Stale vs fresh is decided for the whole clone at once. If even one unpushed event is older than the horizon, the clone is 'stale' and ALL its unpushed events are discarded, including ones written minutes ago. The stated reason ('every write auto-pushes (I5), so the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence') does not hold. An unpushed event only shows that a PUSH has not succeeded since it was written. Inbound convergence (fetch plus union merge in sync) can keep succeeding while a push keeps failing, and a clone with no unpushed events can have last converged at any time. The plan's own no-resurrection rule already shows that replaying uuid-unknown events cannot bring back reclaimed history, so the horizon is not a safety guard here. It only decides how much work is lost.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh' and step 4 'Fresh clones replay; stale clones do not'
scenarios: A clone whose push was refused weeks ago (e.g. a gate rejection) but which has kept merging inbound writes a new ticket today. After the reclaim, today's ticket is discarded together with the old event.
A clone that has been offline for 60 days writes one event yesterday. It is classified fresh, even though by the ADR's definition it is stale.
findings.suggested_fix: Classify per ticket directory. Replay every ticket dir whose unpushed events are all inside the horizon, and discard (and count in the WARNING) only ticket dirs that contain a below-horizon unpushed event, so you never replay an orphaned later event without its earlier ones. Update docs/concurrency.md step 2 to match.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the fresh-clone override atomic: build the replay commit on top of the pinned remote commit with plumbing (temp index + write-tree + commit-tree) before touching HEAD, then move HEAD with a single `reset --hard`, so a failure leaves local state unchanged and retryable.
evidence: Plan: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD ... then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit." followed by "A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
stale_override.py:103-118 runs update-ref, then reset --hard, then _replay (update-index, checkout, commit) as separate fallible steps.
sync.py:_override_if_reclaimed catches StaleOverrideError, logs, and returns True. A later reconverge sees related histories (merge-base exists) and never re-runs the override.
findings.finding: Backup, reset and replay are separate, non-atomic steps: `update-ref` backup, then `reset --hard` to the remote, then update-index/checkout/commit for the replay. If any replay step fails after the reset (commit failure, signing config, disk, index lock), the clone is left on the remote tip without its fresh events. On the next sync HEAD shares history with the remote, so the related-history path runs and the override is never retried. The fresh work survives only in the backup ref, and the only signal is a log line. A more robust approach with the same footprint: build the replay commit with plumbing first (temporary GIT_INDEX_FILE, read-tree of the pinned remote commit, update-index --cacheinfo for the captured blobs, write-tree, commit-tree -p <remote>), then do ONE `reset --hard` to the finished commit. If building fails, nothing local has changed and the next sync can retry.
findings.location: Approach step 3 'Backup, then override' / step 4; src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py
scenarios: `git commit` fails during replay (e.g. commit.gpgsign=true with no key, or an index.lock left by a crashed process). The fresh clone is now permanently on the remote tip and its unpushed events are recoverable only by hand from refs/rebar/stale-override/*.
findings.suggested_fix: In override_onto_reclaimed_remote: capture blobs; if there are any, use a temporary GIT_INDEX_FILE, `read-tree <remote_commit>`, `update-index --add --cacheinfo` for each live path, `write-tree`, `commit-tree <tree> -p <remote_commit> -m ...`, and use that new commit (or remote_commit when nothing is replayed) as the single reset target after the backup update-ref. Add a test that makes the commit step fail and asserts HEAD is unchanged.

evidence: Plan: "Parse event filenames per the I2 contract (`{ts}-{uuid}-{TYPE}.json`, optional `.retired`...)" with only matching files as replay candidates

src/rebar/_commands/delete.py:358-361 writes `.tombstone.json` and appends it to the written set; delete.py:205 and :305 read it to decide tombstoned state
findings.finding: Fresh replay only re-adds files that match the I2 event-filename regex, but rebar also commits non-event marker files in ticket directories as part of the same logical write. `rebar delete` writes `.tombstone.json` next to its STATUS/ARCHIVED events, and readers check that marker (delete.py:205, :305). A fresh clone's unpushed delete would be replayed as events with no tombstone marker, so the replayed state differs from what was written. The plan's 'byte-identically' guarantee covers event files only, and it does not say what happens to committed non-event changes in a fresh clone.
findings.location: Approach step 1 'Local-only events' / step 4 fresh replay
scenarios: A fresh clone deletes a ticket while offline, then reconnects after a reclaim. The STATUS and ARCHIVED events are replayed but `.tombstone.json` is not, so the delete is not idempotent and the ticket-scan filter treats the ticket as not tombstoned.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define a retention policy for `refs/rebar/stale-override/*` (e.g. expire after the reclaim horizon, or keep only the newest) and document how operators recover from or prune them.
evidence: Plan: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed)" — no pruning, expiry, or cap is mentioned anywhere in Scope or Testing.
ADR 0106 Consequences: the purpose is that the pack shrinks in proportion to the reclaimed commit/tree count.
findings.finding: Every override creates a new `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` ref, and the plan sets no retention or expiry for it. Each such ref keeps the clone's whole pre-reclaim history reachable, so local gc can never reclaim it, and refs pile up with each reclaim cycle. Reclaiming that history is the whole point of ADR 0106, so the local clone keeps the object load the reclaim removed from the remote.
findings.location: Approach step 3 'Backup, then override'
scenarios: A long-lived developer clone that goes through several reclaim cycles keeps one full pre-reclaim history per cycle and never shrinks locally.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say what happens when a fresh-clone replay fails after `reset --hard`: compute the replay set before the reset and either roll back to the backup ref on failure, or make the next reconverge detect a backup ref that has not been replayed and finish the replay. evidence: Plan: 'Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD ..., then reset --hard to the pinned remote commit.'
Plan: 'A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files byte-identically ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote'
Absence: the Testing section lists no case where the replay fails after the reset, and the plan does not say how the caller handles that failure.
findings.finding: Fresh-clone replay is not resumable after a partial failure. The plan orders the steps as backup, `reset --hard`, then replay in one commit, but does not say what happens if the replay (staging or commit) fails after the reset. HEAD would then sit on the remote, sharing history with it. On the next reconverge the 'no merge-base + superseding epoch' trigger would not fire again. The clone's unpushed in-horizon events would be left only in the backup ref, with no retry and no warning that replay did not finish.
findings.location: Approach steps 3-4 ('Backup, then override' / 'Fresh clones replay'); Testing section
scenarios: The replay commit fails (disk full, a commit hook, git index lock) after `reset --hard` succeeded: the next sync sees normal shared history, pushes nothing, and the clone's recent unpushed tickets are silently missing from the shared store.
A process crash between the reset and the commit leaves a half-staged index on top of the remote tip.
findings.suggested_fix: If the replay fails, run `reset --hard <backup_ref>` (restoring the pre-override state so the existing DIVERGED refusal applies and the override can be retried), or record replay-pending state next to the backup ref so the next reconverge finishes the replay. Cover either choice with a fault-injection unit test.

evidence: Plan: 'The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days`'

findings.finding: Staleness is decided once for the whole clone: 'stale iff its oldest unpushed event's ts is older than now − horizon', and then 'A stale clone replays nothing'. A clone that has kept syncing but has one old event that never pushed (for example a push that kept failing) is therefore classified stale. Its newer unpushed events, well inside the horizon, are thrown away along with the old one. The plan's justification ('the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence') assumes every write auto-pushes successfully, which is not guaranteed.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('Stale vs fresh') and step 4

Absence: no test or AC asserts the invariant that every reclaimed uuid stays known on the remote, which classification depends on.
findings.finding: The test for whether an event is unpushed (and so the resurrection guard and the stale/fresh decision) only works if the rewritten baseline keeps every reclaimed event uuid, either as a file in the ticket dir or in a SNAPSHOT's `data.source_event_uuids`. The plan states no such invariant for `superseding_record` or for S2's publish-swap baseline. A reclaim that drops a pushed event's file without listing its uuid in a SNAPSHOT's source list would make that event look unpushed. A fresh clone would then replay (resurrect) it. Or its old timestamp would flip the clone to stale and discard real recent writes.

Plan step 4: 'A stale clone replays nothing and logs a WARNING naming the backup ref and the discarded event count' — git-annex chose differently and propagates the rewrite while keeping local data.

Retrieved: git-annex-forget(1) (man.archlinux.org/man/git-annex-forget.1.en; git-annex.branchable.com/git-annex-forget/): 'When this rewritten branch is merged into other clones of the repository, git-annex will automatically perform the same rewriting to their local git-annex branches. So the forgetfulness will automatically propagate out from its starting point until all repositories running git-annex have forgotten their old history.'
Retrieved: git-annex 7.20191017 changelog (hackage.haskell.org/package/git-annex-7.20191017/changelog): 'Fix git-annex branch data loss that could occur after git-annex forget --drop-dead.'

Retrieved: git-rebase docs § 'Recovering from upstream rebase' (git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase), on downstream recovery after an upstream rewrite (the --fork-point mode uses the reflog to find the split point, per the stackoverflow.com/questions/4084868 summary).
ABSENCE: neither the plan nor ADR 0106 §5 / § Alternatives considered names any external design for reconnecting after a rewrite.
findings.finding: The plan builds a new reconnect-after-rewrite protocol (an `epoch_lineage` succession proof, uuid set-difference to find unpushed events, and a stale/fresh split where stale work is discarded) without considering established external prior art for the same problem. The closest analog is git-annex forget, which prunes the history of an auto-synced log branch and spreads the rewrite to clones by re-applying it to each local branch and merging. That keeps local changes instead of discarding them. git-annex also shipped a fix for branch data loss in exactly this propagation path, which makes it a concrete failure mode to test against. The git-rebase 'Recovering from upstream rebase' / --fork-point approach (finding the split point from the reflog) is a second established technique that the plan does not mention.
findings.location: Plan § Approach (steps 1–4) and § Context / Problem; ADR 0106 § Alternatives considered (covers only the collapse, not reconnect)
scenarios: A clone that has been offline more than N days holds valuable unpushed events that are not in the remote's SNAPSHOT `source_event_uuids` and not retired. The plan discards them (they are kept only in a local backup ref). Under git-annex's re-apply-and-merge approach they would have survived, because the uuid no-resurrection rule already blocks reintroducing anything reclaimed.
Rewrite propagation drops data in an edge case like the one git-annex fixed in 7.20191017, and the test matrix doesn't cover it because that failure mode was never looked at.
findings.suggested_fix: In § Approach, add a 'Prior art considered' paragraph. (1) Cite git-annex forget (git-annex.branchable.com/git-annex-forget/) as the closest analog: a rewrite recorded in the branch, re-applied by each clone, then merged. Say why rebar instead discards stale unpushed work, or note that the uuid set-difference filter already blocks resurrection, so stale replay could be safe and the ADR §5 residual could shrink. (2) Cite git-rebase 'Recovering from upstream rebase' as the git-native downstream-recovery pattern, and explain why event-uuid set difference replaces fork-point and patch-id matching (events are content-addressed by uuid, and the reflog cannot be trusted across clones). (3) Note the git-annex 7.20191017 data-loss fix after `forget --drop-dead`, and say which test in tests/unit/test_stale_clone_override.py covers the matching failure mode, or add one.

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
